title: Value & reference types
summary: Know what gets copied when you pass a value, an object, or a reference.
explanation: A value-type variable holds its value. Assigning it copies that value. A reference-type variable holds a reference to an object; assigning it copies the reference, so both variables can point at the same object. Value types are not always on the stack: a struct field inside a class lives inside that heap object. Strings are reference types but immutable.
why: These rules explain unexpected mutations, parameter behavior, boxing costs, and the difference between object identity and equality.
useCase: Two parts of an order-processing service receive the same mutable Order instance. A status change in one is visible to the other. A small immutable Money value, by contrast, can safely represent an amount without shared mutable state.
whenToUse: Use classes for identity and mutable entities. Use small, preferably immutable structs for values. Use ref or out only when the method must work with the caller's variable itself, not merely the object it refers to.
pitfalls: Assuming every value type is allocated on the stack.
Thinking passing a reference-type argument by value prevents object mutation.
Boxing a value type repeatedly through object or a non-generic API.
bestPractices: Make value objects immutable.
Prefer generic APIs to avoid unnecessary boxing.
Distinguish value equality from ReferenceEquals in your explanation.
takeaways: Assignment copies a value or a reference, depending on the type.
Storage location is not the definition of value versus reference type.
Immutability reduces surprises from shared state.

interview.question: Can a method mutate an object passed without ref?
interview.answer: Yes. It receives a copy of the reference and can mutate that same object. Reassigning its parameter to a different object does not reassign the caller's variable.

interview.question: What is boxing?
interview.answer: Boxing wraps a value-type value in an object allocation. Unboxing extracts the original value type. Frequent boxing can create allocation pressure.

quiz.question: After assigning a List<string> to another variable, what is copied?
options: A reference to the same list
quiz.explanation: List<T> is a reference type. Assignment copies its reference, so mutations are visible through both variables.

quiz.question: Where does a struct field of a heap-allocated class instance live?
quiz.explanation: A struct's storage follows its containing location. It can be inline in an object, array, or local storage.

title: Object-oriented thinking
summary: Use encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism to model behavior.
explanation: Encapsulation protects state behind operations. Abstraction exposes what callers need and hides how it works. Inheritance specializes an existing type. Polymorphism lets different implementations satisfy the same contract. An interface is a capability contract; an abstract class can also carry shared state and implementation.
why: Objects keep business rules near the data they protect. Contracts let callers use behavior without coupling themselves to every implementation.
useCase: An online checkout supports card and bank payments. The checkout depends on IPaymentGateway, while each gateway knows its own provider API. An Order exposes Confirm instead of letting any caller set arbitrary status values.
whenToUse: Use composition and interfaces when behavior varies independently. Use inheritance only for a genuine substitutable is-a relationship. Do not create a deep hierarchy just to reuse a few lines.
pitfalls: Public setters that let callers violate business invariants.
Inheritance that forces a subtype to reject the base contract.
Interfaces for every class without a useful boundary.
bestPractices: Keep invariants inside domain operations.
Prefer composition when requirements change along multiple dimensions.
Depend on a small capability, not a large concrete object.
takeaways: Encapsulation protects invariants, not just private fields.
Polymorphism substitutes behavior through a stable contract.
Composition is usually easier to change than deep inheritance.

interview.question: Interface or abstract class?
interview.answer: Use an interface for a capability that unrelated types can implement. Use an abstract class when a real type family needs shared state or a template implementation. C# supports multiple interfaces but one base class.

interview.question: What is runtime polymorphism?
interview.answer: A call through a base type or interface is dispatched to the concrete implementation. Overriding virtual members is different from compile-time overload resolution.

quiz.question: Which design best protects an account balance?
quiz.explanation: Encapsulated operations can enforce the account's invariants before changing its state.

quiz.question: Two unrelated types need the same capability. Start with:
quiz.explanation: A small interface expresses the shared capability without inventing a false inheritance relationship.

title: Choosing the right collection
summary: Match your data structure to lookup, ordering, uniqueness, and concurrency needs.
explanation: List<T> is a growable ordered array: indexing is O(1), but searching is O(n). Dictionary<TKey,TValue> provides average O(1) key lookup. HashSet<T> enforces uniqueness with average O(1) membership checks. Queue<T> is FIFO; Stack<T> is LIFO. These complexities assume normal hashing behavior and are not absolute worst-case guarantees.
why: The right collection makes intent clear and prevents a repeated linear search from turning a simple loop into an O(n squared) bottleneck.
useCase: Importing customer records requires detecting duplicate email addresses. A HashSet with an explicit comparer avoids rescanning every previously imported record. A dictionary maps product IDs to prices for an order calculation.
whenToUse: Use List for ordered iteration, Dictionary for keyed lookup, HashSet for membership, and concurrent collections for shared multi-threaded access. IReadOnlyList limits the consumer API but does not make the underlying object immutable.
pitfalls: Calling Contains on a large list inside another loop.
Mutating a collection during enumeration.
Using mutable dictionary keys or assuming normal collections are thread-safe.
bestPractices: Choose a comparer explicitly for case-insensitive keys.
Use TryGetValue when absence is expected.
Preallocate capacity for a known large batch when profiling supports it.
takeaways: Choose for the dominant operation, not habit.
Hash-based lookups are average O(1), not a universal guarantee.
Read-only access is not the same as immutability.

interview.question: List versus HashSet?
interview.answer: A list preserves indexed order and allows duplicates. A hash set focuses on unique membership and efficient lookup. Use a list when position matters and a set when uniqueness or membership matters.

interview.question: Is Dictionary safe for concurrent writes?
interview.answer: No. Coordinate access with a lock or use ConcurrentDictionary. Even with a concurrent collection, a sequence of operations is not automatically one atomic operation.

quiz.question: Which collection best supports repeated membership tests and uniqueness?
quiz.explanation: HashSet<T> directly models uniqueness and provides average constant-time membership tests.

quiz.question: What does IReadOnlyList<T> guarantee?
options: No other code can mutate the backing collection
The consumer has no mutation members through this interface
quiz.explanation: The interface restricts access. It does not freeze or copy the underlying collection.

title: Generics & type constraints
summary: Write reusable, type-safe code without converting everything to object.
explanation: A generic type or method has type parameters supplied by the caller. List<int> and List<string> share a design but enforce different types. Constraints describe what a type argument must support. Variance allows certain conversions for generic interfaces and delegates: out is covariant output, in is contravariant input, and neither applies to arbitrary mutable classes.
why: Generics catch type mistakes at compile time, avoid many casts and boxing operations, and let reusable algorithms keep meaningful contracts.
useCase: An API uses a Result<T> envelope for either a typed success or a structured failure. A shared validation method can require an interface rather than inspecting objects at runtime.
whenToUse: Use a generic when the algorithm or container is truly independent of the exact type. Add the narrowest constraints needed. Prefer a concrete type if the logic is specific to one domain object.
pitfalls: Using object and casts instead of a type parameter.
Adding new() when a factory or injected dependency is more appropriate.
Assuming List<Derived> is assignable to List<Base>.
bestPractices: Use descriptive type parameters for multiple roles.
Constrain on behavior, not an unnecessarily specific base class.
Remember that variance conversions work with reference types.
takeaways: Generics preserve type information across reusable code.
Constraints make permitted operations explicit.
IEnumerable<out T> can be covariant; mutable List<T> is invariant.

interview.question: Why use generics instead of object?
interview.answer: Generics provide compile-time type safety and reduce casts. Generic collections of value types also avoid the boxing that occurs when values are stored as object.

interview.question: Why is List<T> invariant?
interview.answer: A list both accepts and returns T. If a List<Dog> could become List<Animal>, a caller could insert a Cat into a dog-only list. A producer-only interface can safely be covariant.

quiz.question: What does where TEntity : IIdentifiable establish?
quiz.explanation: The constraint lets the generic implementation use IIdentifiable members without runtime casts.

quiz.question: Why can IEnumerable<Dog> be used as IEnumerable<Animal> for reference types?
quiz.explanation: IEnumerable<out T> produces values of T without accepting arbitrary T values from the consumer.

title: Delegates, lambdas & events
summary: Pass behavior as a value and notify subscribers without coupling to them.
explanation: A delegate is a type-safe reference to a compatible method. Func returns a value; Action returns void. A lambda is concise syntax for an anonymous function, and may capture surrounding variables. An event wraps a delegate so outside code can subscribe or unsubscribe but cannot raise it directly.
why: These tools separate an algorithm from a chosen behavior and let publishers announce changes without knowing all subscribers.
useCase: A pricing engine receives a discount function. A desktop model raises a changed event so multiple views can react. A long-lived event publisher must not accidentally retain a discarded subscriber.
whenToUse: Use delegates for callbacks and small strategies; use events for in-process notifications. Use a durable broker for cross-process events, not a C# event. Prefer Task-returning delegates for asynchronous workflows.
pitfalls: Forgetting to unsubscribe from a longer-lived publisher.
Capturing a mutable variable and expecting a frozen value.
Using async void outside an event-handler boundary.
bestPractices: Keep callback contracts small and explicit.
Unsubscribe using the same delegate instance.
Decide how subscriber exceptions should affect the publisher.
takeaways: A lambda creates a function, not automatically a new thread.
An event restricts who may invoke the underlying delegate.
Captured variables and subscriptions have lifetime consequences.

interview.question: Delegate versus event?
interview.answer: A delegate holds invocable method references. An event exposes subscription semantics and reserves invocation for the declaring type, protecting the publisher's notification contract.

interview.question: What is a closure?
interview.answer: A function plus captured surrounding state. It captures variables rather than taking an automatic value snapshot, and can extend the captured state's lifetime.

quiz.question: What may outside code do with a public event?
quiz.explanation: Events expose add/remove access. Only the declaring type controls raising a normal event.

quiz.question: Which delegate represents an async operation with no result value?
quiz.explanation: Func<Task> lets the caller await completion and observe exceptions. An async Action becomes async void.

title: LINQ & deferred execution
summary: Describe data transformations, then know when and where they actually run.
explanation: LINQ composes filtering, projection, grouping, and aggregation. Many IEnumerable operators use deferred execution: enumeration runs the pipeline. ToList materializes results immediately. IQueryable builds expression trees for a provider, such as EF Core, to translate. Not every C# expression can become SQL.
why: LINQ makes transformations readable, but understanding execution prevents duplicate work, unexpected results after mutation, and accidental database round trips.
useCase: An order endpoint filters paid orders, projects only the fields a screen needs, and materializes once. The filter and projection should happen in the database rather than after downloading the entire Orders table.
whenToUse: Use LINQ for clear data transformations. Materialize when you need a stable snapshot or repeated enumeration. Keep queries provider-translatable until the deliberate database boundary.
pitfalls: Enumerating an expensive query multiple times.
Calling ToList before a selective database filter.
Using First when no match is a normal outcome, or hiding invalid uniqueness with FirstOrDefault.
bestPractices: Project only required columns.
Use Any for existence and Single when uniqueness is an invariant.
Inspect generated SQL for important EF queries.
takeaways: Defining a deferred query is different from enumerating it.
IEnumerable runs .NET iteration; IQueryable delegates translation to a provider.
Materialization is an intentional boundary.

interview.question: IEnumerable versus IQueryable?
interview.answer: IEnumerable exposes iteration over values. IQueryable also carries an expression tree that a provider can translate, often to SQL. Calling AsEnumerable moves subsequent operations to ordinary .NET enumeration; it does not itself materialize the query.

interview.question: What can change between two enumerations?
interview.answer: The source data or captured variables may change, and expensive operations may run again. ToList creates a snapshot of the sequence at that point, though referenced objects inside can still be mutable.

quiz.question: When does Where over a List usually evaluate its predicate?
quiz.explanation: Where is deferred. Enumeration, such as foreach or ToList, causes predicates to run.

quiz.question: Which order usually avoids loading unnecessary database rows?
quiz.explanation: Keep the filter in the IQueryable pipeline so the provider can translate it before materializing results.

title: Exceptions & resilient boundaries
summary: Handle failures where you can recover, and preserve the evidence when you cannot.
explanation: Exceptions propagate until a compatible catch handles them. Finally runs during normal control-flow unwinding and is useful for cleanup, while using is preferred for IDisposable resources. Use throw; to rethrow without resetting the original stack trace. Expected business outcomes such as a declined payment are often clearer as explicit results.
why: A deliberate error boundary keeps failures understandable, avoids hiding defects, and prevents internal implementation details from leaking to users.
useCase: An API translates an unknown order into 404 and unexpected server failures into a safe Problem Details response. A worker retries selected transient network failures but does not retry invalid credentials forever.
whenToUse: Throw for exceptional or invalid states. Catch when you can recover, add useful context, or translate at a boundary. Let cancellation remain cancellation rather than reporting it as an ordinary server failure.
pitfalls: Swallowing Exception with an empty catch.
Using throw caughtException and losing the original throw location.
Retrying non-transient or non-idempotent operations indiscriminately.
bestPractices: Catch the most specific exception you can handle.
Log once at the responsible boundary with structured context.
Use using or await using for deterministic resource cleanup.
takeaways: Recover locally or translate at an explicit boundary.
Rethrow with throw; to preserve the stack.
Cancellation and expected business failures need deliberate treatment.

interview.question: throw versus throw exception?
interview.answer: Inside a catch, throw; preserves the original exception stack. Throwing the caught variable resets its throw location. Wrap with an inner exception only when a new abstraction-level message adds meaning.

interview.question: Should every method catch Exception?
interview.answer: No. Catching without recovery or useful translation adds noise and may hide defects. Central boundaries can log and translate otherwise unhandled exceptions.

quiz.question: Which statement preserves the original exception stack inside catch?
quiz.explanation: A bare throw rethrows the current exception while preserving its original stack trace.

quiz.question: Invalid user input is expected frequently. Prefer:
options: Exceptions as the normal parser branch
quiz.explanation: TryParse models an ordinary unsuccessful parse without using exceptions for expected control flow.

title: Records, nullability & pattern matching
summary: Make data shapes and missing-value rules visible in your types.
explanation: Records provide generated value-based equality and convenient non-destructive updates with with expressions. Record classes remain reference types, and nested mutable members are not made deeply immutable. Nullable reference annotations let the compiler track possible nulls; they are warnings and contracts, not automatic runtime validation. Patterns express shape and value checks concisely.
why: Clear types reduce null-reference surprises and make request, response, and value-object code easier to reason about.
useCase: A checkout response is an immutable-looking snapshot represented by a record. An optional delivery note is string?, while required external input is still validated at the HTTP boundary.
whenToUse: Use records for data-centric values and DTOs. Enable nullable reference types for new code. Use patterns for readable branching over known cases, not as a replacement for every polymorphic design.
pitfalls: Using ! to silence a warning instead of proving the value is present.
Assuming a record containing a List is deeply immutable.
Treating the required keyword as full runtime validation of incoming JSON.
bestPractices: Validate external input even when annotations look non-nullable.
Use immutable members when relying on stable value semantics.
Handle unknown or unmatched cases deliberately.
takeaways: Record class means reference type with generated value equality.
Nullable annotations guide the compiler; validate untrusted input at runtime.
A with copy is shallow.

interview.question: Does a with expression deep-copy a record?
interview.answer: No. It copies the record's members, then applies changes. Reference-type members still refer to the same nested objects unless replaced explicitly.

interview.question: Does string prevent null at runtime?
interview.answer: No. With nullable reference types enabled, string expresses a non-null intent and produces compiler diagnostics for suspicious code. Reflection, deserialization, legacy code, and null-forgiving operators can still violate it.

quiz.question: A record contains List<string>. What does a with copy do to that list?
quiz.explanation: Record copying is shallow; nested references are shared unless explicitly replaced.

quiz.question: What does the null-forgiving operator ! do?
quiz.explanation: The operator changes compiler flow analysis, not the runtime value or behavior.
